articles.summary: Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined.
articles.summary_zh: 从2016年到2018年,我是一个社交媒体正义战士. 我花时间在Facebook和Twitter上, 如果你读到我的文章,你可能没有猜到我在郊区一个保守的基督教家庭长大,或者我从4岁开始每天在基督教学校接受教育。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度.
articles.title_zh: 我是一名正义战士。我需要完整的福音。你也是。
articles.content: From 2016 to 2018, I was a social media justice warrior. I spent my time on Facebook and Twitter confronting the powerful and comfortable, championing justice issues, and fighting for racial and political reconciliation. If you read my posts, you might not have guessed that I grew up in a conservative Christian home nestled in suburbia, or that I spent every day of my education, starting at age 4, in Christian schools. In my upbringing, I learned the rich depths of the Christian faith. I surrendered my life to Jesus, and I learned that Jesus came to seek to save the lost. Yet that evangelistically oriented world of my youth was intentionally sanitized and separated from the painful realities of poverty and injustice just 10 minutes down the road. When I discovered this disparity, I became a justice warrior online. And while that posture was certainly a reaction to my upbringing, I wasn’t being a hypocrite. My social media advocacy reflected my actual life. I’ve lived and worked in an underresourced neighborhood since 2001. During my first 15 years in the neighborhood, I grew burdened over the disconnect I saw between the conditions my neighbors faced daily and how many in the American church live. The political, racial, and socioeconomic divide between my church life and neighborhood gutted me. So when I went online, I was convinced I was sharing the true gospel. Yet that “gospel” I shared was merely centered on producing tangible results in the here and now, not on affecting eternity. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. Two Gospel Aspects I began to see two aspects in the biblical gospel. Let’s call them the gospel of the cross and the gospel of the kingdom . The gospel of the cross is the good news that Jesus Christ saves and adopts believers as his children through his substitutionary death and glorious resurrection. We’re all born alienated from God. In sin, we’re his enemies. In Christ, as we believe the good news, we’re reconciled to God (Rom. 5:6–10) and assured of eternal life with him (John 3:16). As Peter writes, “Christ also suffered once for sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God” (1 Pet. 3:18). Moreover, the cross aspect of the gospel emphasizes that those entrusted with this message must share it with a lost and dying world (Matt. 28:18–20). The gospel of the cross must be heralded; it must be proclaimed. It is the priority. From this gospel flows every good gift. What I needed instead was a holistic gospel, one that centers around both God’s kingdom mission and also his sacrificial death for sinners on the cross. The gospel of the kingdom is the good news that God’s will for justice, goodness, and peace is already being unleashed. As God’s children, believers are invited to play a part in seeing that kingdom mission come to fruition. Jesus begins his ministry by preaching a message that proclaims “good news to the poor” and “liberty to the . . . oppressed” (Luke 4:18). He calls his hearers to repent, including from ways they’ve oppressed and neglected the poor (Matt. 3:2; 4:17). He specifically rebukes the Pharisees for neglecting “the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness” (23:23). Paul, too, teaches that the gospel not only reunites us to God but also works justice by reconciling divided peoples to one another in the church. He writes, “For [Christ] himself is our peace, who has made us both [ethnic groups] one and has broken down in his flesh the dividing wall of hostility” (Eph. 2:14). We fulfill the law and live out the gospel’s kingdom implications through our identity as shalom -makers (Matt. 5:9). The kingdom aspect of the gospel equips us with a vision for pursuing God’s will “on earth as it is in heaven” (6:10), that is, for seeing all things made new (Rev. 21:5). This gospel of the kingdom must be lived out through embodied action. Mapping Our Approaches to Cross and Kingdom Most Christians today rightly see these two gospel aspects—the message proper and its kingdom implications—as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined. As a result, many emphasize only one aspect or the other. And sadly, some neglect both these aspects of the gospel altogether. Nicholas Wolterstorff writes that shalom is “a harmony and delight in all of one’s relationships: between us and God, us and other people, us and other cultures, us and creation, and between us and our very selves.” In the four-quadrant grid below, I’ve mapped out the ways we typically approach the cross and kingdom aspects of the gospel. (For more, see section II.3 of The Gospel Coalition’s Theological Vision for Ministry .) Christ’s sacrifice on the cross restores us to harmony and delight with God. This is our most important relationship, and it’s represented on the diagram by the upward-pointing vertical axis. A kingdom emphasis on harmony and delight in other people, other cultures, and the creation is represented by the rightward-pointing horizontal axis. Quadrants II and IV represent two errors—the false choice of emphasizing either the cross or kingdom while neglecting the other. Many American Christians have been ensnared by one of these two quadrants. Quadrant III designates a total neglect of both cross and also kingdom. All these disconnects result from misunderstanding who a Christian is and what a Christian should do in this broken world. Quadrant IV: Individualized Gospel Advocates of an individualized gospel (quadrant IV) want to get people saved for the afterlife without stressing the social implications for this life. When sinners are saved, we always celebrate! However, Christians who fit in this quadrant often don’t emphasize the kingdom aspect of the gospel. Such individuals and churches may financially support ministries in underresourced neighborhoods but don’t often emphasize transformative service there. Many such churches and their members may not understand or appreciate the depth and range of problems in struggling communities, even in neighborhoods not far from them. Quadrant II: Social Gospel Advocates of the social gospel seek to meet people’s imminent needs but neglect their ultimate need of the salvation Jesus offers. This is a scandalous compromise, and it’s the false gospel I believed for nearly a decade and then proclaimed as a social media justice warrior. My wife and I moved into our underresourced neighborhood to live close to the school where I served for 18 years. Living and working among the poor showed me that many people need more than hearing about Jesus alone. They needed tangible help. Many of my quadrant IV friends concluded my neighbors were ignorant, dangerous, and to be avoided. So I reacted to my peers by propelling myself into the social gospel. Most Christians today see these two gospel aspects as part of the same biblical pie. But we often fail to see them as necessarily intertwined. The social gospel is an late 19th- and early 20th-century theological movement focused on breaking the chains of oppression and championing the poor. Advocates seek to make Christ’s kingdom manifest on earth through acts of charity, philanthropy, and just legislation. Some social-gospel advocates choose to live close to the poor to improve their neighborhoods and lives. Yet the social gospel focuses solely on meeting imminent needs. It neglects preaching Christ as the sinner’s Savior. In fact, many social-gospel advocates reject the evangelical gospel and biblical authority. Many parachurch organizations that serve underresourced communities are held hostage by social-gospel theology. Though the leaders may be Christians, you can scour the organizations’ websites and messaging yet find no evidence of an orthodox theological foundation. 如果你读到我的文章,你可能没有猜到我在郊区一个保守的基督教家庭长大,或者我从4岁开始每天在基督教学校接受教育。 在我成长的过程中,我学会了基督教信仰的丰富深度. 我把自己的生命交给了耶稣,我得知耶稣是来寻求拯救失落者.
然而,我青年中以福音为取向的世界被故意洗涤,并在10分钟后脱离了贫穷和不公正的痛苦现实。 当我发现这种差距,我成为在线上的正义战士。 虽然这种姿态无疑是对我成长的反应, 我的社交媒体宣传反映了我的真实生活.
我从2001年起就住在资源不足的街区工作。 在附近15年里, 我对邻居每天面临的状况 和美国教会中有多少人的生活脱节感到负担沉重。 我的教会生活和邻居之间的政治、种族和社会经济鸿沟使我心碎。
所以当我上网时,我确信我分享了真正的福音。 然而,我所分享的“神灵”仅仅集中于在这里和现在产生实际结果,而不是影响永恒。 我所需要的是一个整体的福音,它既围绕上帝的王国使命,也围绕他为十字架上罪人而牺牲的死亡。
我开始在圣经福音书中看到两个方面。 让我们把他们称为十字架和王国的福音。 十字架的福音是好消息,耶稣基督通过他的替代死亡和光荣的复活来拯救并接纳信徒作为他的孩子. 我们天生都与上帝隔绝。 我们是他的敌人,
在基督中,我们相信好消息,因此与上帝和解(5:6-10),并与他保证永生(John 3:16). 正如彼得所写道的,“耶稣也曾因罪孽而受苦;正义者为不义之人所受苦,以便他能把我们带到上帝面前”(第3:18页)。

尼古拉斯·沃尔特斯托夫(Nicholas Wolterstorff)写道:"在一个人的所有关系中,我们与上帝、我们与其他人、我们与其他文化、我们与创造之间,以及我们与我们自身之间,都是和谐和愉快的"。 在下面的四平地网格中, 我绘制了我们一般处理福音的十字和王国方面的方式。

articles.title: Lessons from Lloyd-Jones on Preaching and Politics
articles.summary: Here are three lessons we can learn from Martyn Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis.
articles.summary_zh: “我从未担心过像希特勒这样的人。 ” 这不是一个疯子或有权免于战争恐怖的人的说法。 这些是一位牧师的话,他受到纳粹领导人的直接威胁,他穿上了神的全盔并准备出战。 阿道夫·希特勒于1939年9月1日入侵波兰;
articles.title_zh: 劳埃德-琼斯关于讲道和政治的教训
articles.content: “I was never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” This isn’t the statement of a madman or of someone privileged enough to be removed from the horrors of the war. These are the words of a pastor who was under immediate threat from the Nazi leader and who’d put on the full armor of God and prepared for battle. Adolf Hitler invaded Poland on September 1, 1939; the very next day, Martyn Lloyd-Jones was installed as an associate pastor at Westminster Chapel in London, where he would faithfully preach for the next 30 years. One year after the preacher took the pulpit, Hitler began his bombing campaign over London. Of the roughly 700 churches in the area, 624 were damaged by the bombings and 91 were totally destroyed. To the surprise of many, Westminster Chapel, one of London’s largest churches at the time, wasn’t destroyed in the bombing blitz. Iain Murray, in his classic biography on Lloyd-Jones , writes about one Sunday morning when a bomb hit close to the Chapel right in the middle of Lloyd-Jones’s Lord’s Day prayer. The bomb shook the entire building, and plaster and dust fell down on the congregation, including on “the Doctor,” as Lloyd-Jones was known. After a pause, Lloyd-Jones simply continued his prayer and the service went forward unimpeded. Lloyd-Jones offers a needed corrective to our politically anxious times. Some Christians resort to despair, while others attempt revolution. What we need is a political theology that still preaches Christ when the bombs go off. Here are three lessons we can learn from Lloyd-Jones’s ministry in a time of political crisis. Refuse Saul’s Armour When it became apparent that England was entering the war, Lloyd-Jones sent his wife and their two children back to Wales and away from the city, not knowing what would become of it. In a brief and urgent correspondence to his wife, he writes , “Leave yourself and me too, and everything in God’s hand and you will find peace and rest.” With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. With bombs flying overhead, many in the church were calling for a revolution, but Lloyd-Jones was calling for prayer. Because of fear and panic, many began to abandon the weapons of the church and replace them with the weapons of the state. But Lloyd-Jones refused to blur the lines. When the war was at its worst and his congregation had been reduced to few because of death and displacement, he remained resolute in affirming 2 Corinthians 10:4: “The weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (KJV). Lloyd-Jones refused to allow revolutionary alliances and tactics to infiltrate the church: Alas, far too often the church has tried to meet the world and its persecuting power with like weapons to those employed by the enemy. She has made alliances with the state and she has tried to strengthen herself in a material sense. She has been slow to discover what David discovered long ago in his fight with Goliath, that she cannot fight in the armour of Saul, but must ever use her own weapons with which she is familiar and with which she is meant to use. Lloyd-Jones saw a parallel between those in Saul’s armory who were looking to outfit David for battle with new calls from within the church to align herself with the state. Like David’s pitiful sling, prayer may appear in the world’s eyes woefully insufficient weaponry against fascism. But God’s weapons are greater than the weapons of men. Reject the Partisan Gospel Lloyd-Jones saw that the church was particularly vulnerable to political idolatry when fear had gripped the people. Like the Israelites shaking at the sight of Goliath, we often feel the only reasonable response is to find our own “strong man” to fight our battles. Throughout the church’s history, we’ve often turned to national politics. In a talk titled “ Living in Revolutionary Times ,” Lloyd-Jones rebukes the evangelicals of his day, who “seem to think that they are innovators in saying that we should all be taking an interest in politics and social matters.” But this is nothing new. Lloyd-Jones recalls, “They do not seem to have heard of the ‘social gospel’ craze of the earlier part of this century. All this has been tried with great thoroughness.” A preacher unaware of the dangerous pitfalls the church has already fallen into is sure to lead his congregation into one of those pits. This was the great danger, in Lloyd-Jones’s mind, of harnessing power for the church through political means. Any talk of political revolution inside the church—or a call to Christianize the nation—is a call to put on Saul’s armor again. In that same talk, Lloyd-Jones cautions preachers against the temptation to quickly gather a crowd by preaching politics. His words feel even more timely today: I well remember certain men who were concerned about social and political matters, and who constantly preached on such themes, and packed their chapels for a while, but only as long as they preached politics. The moment they began to preach the gospel truly the crowds left them. Politically-minded people are always ready to make use of the church, but they always abandon and shun her when she ceases to be of any value to them. American pulpits have been infected with this kind of partisan preaching for decades now, on both the left and right. It draws crowds but does a disservice to the gospel. It’s important for Christians to offer a robust political and social ethic, but not at the expense of the gospel. The former flows from the latter, and the order is irreversible. Remember the ‘Leaven’ For Lloyd-Jones, spiritual resurrection—not political revolution—would save the world. The church didn’t need a theology of liberation but a theology of “leaven.” Drawing a straight line through the New Testament, he says , “The Christian is represented as ‘salt’ in society and ‘leaven,’ and surely the whole point of those comparisons is that Christian influence is to be a quiet influence and a slow process of influencing society.” Any talk of political revolution inside the church—or a call to Christianize the nation—is a call to put on Saul’s armor again. In times of political crisis, such as our own, we’re tempted to forget this basic biblical principle. We must remember that “the kingdom of God is like leaven” (Matt. 13:33). If we’re to have social and political influence, it’ll only happen through preaching and preserving the gospel, so that regenerate Christians can be salt and light in the public square. On May 21, 1943, when Westminster Chapel was finally seeing signs of stability after the bombings, Lloyd-Jones wrote a letter responding to a congregant who was thanking him for his faithful preaching. He ended by saying , “The supreme need of the hour is intense prayer for spiritual revival on the part of Christian people.” The Doctor was interested in treating the disease, not the symptoms. That’s why he could speak with such audacity, testifying that he was “never worried for a second about a man like Hitler.” As wicked as Hitler was, he was merely symptomatic of the spiritual disease of the human heart—to which the gospel alone is the cure.

articles.content: https://media.thegospelcoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/23102213/effective-evangelism.mp3 In the summer of 2021, pastor Luke Peterson moved to Columbus, Ohio, to look for lost people. To find them, he joined a gym. He started building friendships. And then he began asking those friends if they wanted to come over. “Word started getting around—‘You’re not going to believe this, but Luke’s a pastor,’” he said. ‘It created some intrigue, and people started coming. I used to have a note in my phone of how many people came to our church because I went to CrossFit Grandview. It was up to like 60 or 70 before I stopped counting because it was impossible.” Peterson’s good at evangelism, and his church is too—last year, they welcomed around 500 first-time visitors. When he preaches, he knows about half his audience is probably unchurched. Pastor Luke Peterson (right) chats with Capital Church attendees / Courtesy of Capital Church Facebook This is unusual in a country where 40 million adults have stopped attending church over the last 30 years, and where 76 percent of pastors said “fostering connections with unchurched people” is a need in their church. Much has changed since the Billy Graham rallies of the ’60s, the door-knocking of the ’80s, and seeker-sensitive church billboards of the ’90s. In the past, “you could randomly walk up to the person pumping gas next to you and say, ‘Do you know Jesus?’” said Perimeter Church pastor Jeff Norris. “Could that still work? Sure. But more and more, we tell people to invite neighbors into their home. The reality is that evangelism is much slower, and more relational, than it used to be.” Today, people aren’t as likely to read the Bible, think it’s the Word of God, or go to church . But they’re also less hostile to Christianity than they were five years ago. And while they read the Bible less—especially in Gen Z—the trajectory is moving up . “We’re not past ‘my truth, your truth,’” said Rob Warren, pastor of Doxa Church in Madison, Wisconsin. “But people aren’t as sure that their truth is actually true.” These days, evangelistically effective churches are keeping evangelism front of mind in the way they preach, train, and encourage their congregations. They’re celebrating small wins. And they’re leading with a high view of Scripture, prayer, and God’s sovereignty. “We’ve seen all of our ministries grow—from kids to youth to college ministry to Doxa Church as a whole,” Warren said. “It’s not just one demographic of people who are getting saved. God’s doing something.” Times Have Changed Thirty years ago, evangelical churches leaned on programs like Evangelism Explosion or Continuous Witness Training to deliver evangelistic focus and training, church leader Thom Rainer said . Those structured initiatives fit well in a culture that was more Christian and more institutionalized—it took an average of 20 church members to reach one person for Christ per year. Today, it takes 50, Rainer said . “Evangelism efficacy, evangelism effectiveness, has definitely diminished.” That trend is likely to continue. As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult. As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult. “I’ve got a new couple that moved into my neighborhood a while ago, and I haven’t even seen them yet,” said Daniel Simmons, executive pastor of campuses and central discipleship at The Summit Church. This means equipping the congregation is more challenging—and important—than ever before. “Evangelism can be this thing that is so burdensome and guilt-driven,” said pastor Christian Gracia. He planted King’s City Church in Las Vegas in 2024 with around 80 people and has seen the church grow to more than 400. “People can feel like they’re not ready or not good enough at evangelism,” Gracia said. “They don’t always know what to say, and can feel like a terrible Christian because they don’t do it. And I always want to help them understand that’s not true.” Start with Leadership If church leaders want to create a culture of evangelism in their church, there’s only one place to start, said Warren, who has baptized 150 people in the last eight months. “Tell me 10 people that you’ve shared the gospel with over the last month or two,” he said. “Because if the leadership team is not doing that, then it’s just an aspirational thing and you’re not going to be able to sustain it. You need those ‘just the other day’ stories.” At Perimeter, they’re putting structure around this. This PCA megachurch in Atlanta was planted by a gifted evangelist, Randy Pope, in 1977. Over the years, they’ve seen thousands come to Christ. But last spring, during a staff training, Norris noticed the focus had slipped. “What we tend to do, if left unto ourselves, if church leaders aren’t constantly pushing, is default to what is comfortable,” he said. “Church becomes more about me and my comfort or what my children need. . . . If you don’t constantly keep pushing on evangelism, it’s going to become too big of a burden and people will stop doing it.” Perimeter Church has grown largely through evangelism / Courtesy of Perimeter Church He saw this during Perimeter’s two-day staff workshop: “It became a bit more evident that most of us aren’t making disciples,” he said. “I told them—starting with the executive leadership team all the way down—that their supervisor is going to begin asking them what’s going on in their personal ministry.” This isn’t quota-driven, like “How many times have you shared the gospel this week?” It’s more along the lines of “Who are you praying for who doesn’t know Jesus?” “How are you trusting the Lord to provide opportunities for you to share the gospel with that person?” And then, “Have you been able to have those conversations? If so, how have those gone? Is there anything I can be praying for?” Over at The Summit Church, pastored by evangelist J. D. Greear, similar conversations are taking place. “We only grew 2 percent this year—we have not grown much over the past few years,” Simmons said. “We did some real soul searching in the spring, and found that our people have lost that invitation culture.” So Summit staff are reminding themselves of their goals. “Every ministry needs to know how they contribute to reaching lost people with the gospel, including the ones that may not intuitively do it,” Simmons said. “We’ve got a strong prayer ministry here. How does prayer contribute to reaching lost people? They should know that. Our deacon ministry should know how they contribute to reaching lost people. Our small group ministry should know how they contribute to reaching lost people.” Preaching As leaders begin to share their faith, it’ll come out in their conversations: “Just the other day, I was talking to a guy . . .” This is especially powerful if it comes from the pulpit—and that’s only the beginning of how pastors can use their platform to encourage the spread of the gospel. In a recent sermon, Gracia talked about truth and morality, explaining ideas such as postmodernism and cultural relativism. Christian Gracia preaching at King’s City Church in Las Vegas in October 2026 / Courtesy of King’s City Church YouTube “We’re not trying to win arguments,” he told his congregation. “I’m not trying to give you ammo for the water cooler. articles.title_zh: 我们需要了解我们的改革根源
articles.content: What does it mean to be Reformed? The label is used frequently but not always carefully. For some, it simply refers to a particular view of salvation. For others, it evokes a tradition, a culture, or even an aesthetic. Yet historically, to be Reformed has meant something much richer. While no single sentence can capture the fullness of the Reformed tradition, at minimum it means three things: to be biblical, to be covenantal, and to be confessional. The authority of Scripture governs our theology, covenant theology provides Scripture’s redemptive framework, and the historic confessions summarize and safeguard the church’s doctrinal convictions. Remove any one of those pillars, and something essential to the Reformed tradition is lost. With “Reformed” in its name, it’s hardly surprising that Reformed Theological Seminary has long sought to equip pastors and church members in all three areas. In recent years, members of its faculty have produced substantial volumes on the Old and New Testaments and on covenant theology. Now, with The Westminster Confession of Faith: A Comprehensive Commentary on Its History, Theology, and Application , they turn their attention to the confessional foundation of the Reformed tradition. The result is a volume that seeks not only to explain what the confession teaches but also to demonstrate why confessional theology remains vital for the church today. What Is the Westminster Confession of Faith? The Westminster Confession of Faith takes its name from the Westminster Assembly, a gathering of more than 100 ministers and theologians convened by the English Parliament in 1643 at a time of profound political and ecclesiastical upheaval. The assembly was tasked with recommending reforms to the doctrine, worship, government, and discipline of the Church of England. After more than five years of careful biblical study and theological deliberation, the assembly produced the Westminster Confession of Faith along with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms. Together, these documents have served as the doctrinal foundation of Presbyterian churches throughout the world for nearly four centuries. The assembly’s influence, however, extends far beyond Presbyterianism. The confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. As a result, its theological influence shaped generations of Congregationalists, Baptists, and other evangelical Christians. The editors of this volume rightly observe, The confession is also ecumenical because it found wide acceptance among Congregationalists and Particular Baptists in the seventeenth century, as two different groups of theologians adapted the confession according to their theological convictions, producing the Savoy Declaration (1658) and the Second London Confession (1689). Thus the Westminster Confession is relevant to Presbyterians, Congregationalists, and Baptists. (xx) Why Another Commentary? The Westminster Confession has never lacked commentators. From the 17th century onward, pastors and theologians have written to explain its theology. Quality works by A. A. Hodge , G. I. Williamson, R. C. Sproul, and more recently Chad Van Dixhoorn have each served the church well in different ways. So why do we need another commentary on the confession, and what makes this one useful? The Westminster Confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. First, this isn’t the work of a single author but a collaborative effort by scholars whose expertise spans several areas of theology. That breadth allows the volume to approach the confession from different perspectives while maintaining a clear unity of purpose. Each contributor brings particular expertise to the section he addresses, but the volume as a whole is concerned with helping readers understand the confession and its significance for the church. Second, the commentary is consciously pastoral. Rather than treating the confession merely as a historical artifact or an academic text, the contributors consistently demonstrate how its theology serves the life of the church. Readers are reminded that the confession was written not simply to settle theological disputes but to help the church understand and live out the whole counsel of God. This pastoral emphasis matters. It’s easy for a confession to become something we study without allowing it to shape the way we live as Christians. The Westminster Confession was never intended to be a document we merely admire or defend. Its doctrines are meant to shape the faith of the church as we “contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints” (Jude 1:3). This commentary is useful because it helps readers make that connection, showing not only what the assembly confessed but why those truths matter today. Faith with Roots As a pastor, I’m finding that one of the great needs of our day is a sense of rootedness. Many Christians are looking for something that will give them a deeper sense of stability and connection to the historic Christian faith, something that didn’t begin with the latest movement or cultural moment. They’re looking for something with roots. It’s easy for a confession to become something we study without allowing it to shape the way we live as Christians. This is one of the gifts of the Westminster Confession of Faith. Its doctrinal roots have given generations of believers a lasting stability, keeping them grounded in the historic faith through waves of theological and cultural change. It doesn’t simply teach us what to believe; it roots those beliefs within the life of the church, connecting us to generations of faithful Christians who have confessed these same truths before us. The Westminster Confession helps us to see that we don’t have to find our footing in the Christian faith on our own. We receive the gift of learning from generations of believers who have gone before us, helping us see the riches of Scripture with greater clarity and confidence. This volume is an invitation to rediscover that heritage and to find fresh encouragement in the faithfulness of God, who has sustained his church through the centuries. May it help a new generation find joy in the riches of the Reformed tradition and pass them on with confidence to those who follow.

改革意味着什么? 标签经常使用,但并不总是谨慎。 对有些人来说,它只是指救赎的特定观点. 对其他人来说,它引起一种传统、一种文化,甚至一种美学。 然而,从历史上看,改革意味着更加富有的东西。
虽然没有一句话能够捕捉改革传统的全部,但至少它意味着三件事:圣经,盟约,忏悔. 《圣经》的权威支配着我们的神学,《盟约》神学提供了《圣经》的红发框架,历史的忏悔概括并捍卫了教会的教义信念。
移除其中任何一根支柱,而对于改革后的传统至关重要的东西就失去了。 改革神学院长期试图在所有三个领域为牧师和教会成员提供教具, 近年来,其院系成员编写了大量关于《新旧约》和《盟约》神学的书籍。
现在,随着《威斯敏斯特信仰的忏悔:对其历史、神学和适用的综合评论》,他们把注意力转向了改革后传统的忏悔基础。 结果的一卷不仅试图解释忏悔的教义,还试图说明为什么忏悔神学至今仍然对教会至关重要.
韦斯敏斯特对信仰的忏悔是什么? 威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔会取自威斯敏斯特大会,这是1643年英国议会在政治和宗教剧变深刻时召开的100多名部长和神学家的集会.
议会的任务是建议对英格兰教会的学说,崇拜,政府和纪律进行改革. 经过五年多的认真的圣经研究和神学审议,大会产生了"威斯敏斯特信仰忏悔书"和"大而短的天主教".
近四个世纪以来,这些文件共同成为全世界长老会教会的理论基础。 然而,议会的影响远远超出长老会。 忏悔有助于形成更广泛的改革传统,为后来的忏悔声明提供了框架。
因此,它的神学影响塑造了几代基督教会,浸信会和其他福音派基督徒.
这本书的编辑们正确地指出,《忏悔书》也具有普世性,因为它在17世纪被基督教会和特定浸信会广泛接受,因为两个不同的神学家群体根据他们的神学信念修改了供词,产生了《萨伏伊宣言》(1658年)和《第二次伦敦忏悔书》(1689年)。
因此,威斯敏斯特忏悔与长老会、基督教会和浸信会有关。 (二十) 为什么另作评注? "威斯敏斯特忏悔书"从未缺少评论家. 从17世纪开始,牧师和神学家都撰文解释其神学. 质量作品由A. A. Hodge, G. I. Williamson, R. C.
以及最近查德·范迪克斯霍恩以不同方式为教会服务。 那么,为什么我们需要对供词作另一条评论,是什么使得这一条有用呢? 威斯敏斯特忏悔有助于形成更广泛的改革传统,为后来的忏悔声明提供了框架。
首先,这不是一位作者的作品, 这种宽度使得数量能够从不同的角度对待供词,同时保持明确的目的一致。
每个贡献者都为他所讲的一节带来了特殊的专业知识,但整个卷子都涉及帮助读者理解忏悔及其对教会的意义. 第二,评注是自觉的。
撰稿人不但没有将忏悔仅仅视为历史文物或学术文本,反而一致地表明其神学如何为教会的生活服务. 读者被提醒,供词的写作不仅是为了解决神学上的争议,而且是为了帮助教会理解和活出上帝的整个建议. 这种对牧业的重视很重要。
忏悔很容易成为我们研究的东西, 威斯敏斯特的忏悔从来就不是 我们只崇拜或捍卫的文件 它的教义意在塑造教会的信仰,因为我们“延续着永远交给圣徒的信仰”(Jude 1:3)。
这一评论很有用,因为它有助于读者建立这种联系,不仅表明大会承认了什么,而且表明为什么这些真理今天才重要。 对根的信念 作为牧师,我发现我们这个时代的巨大需求之一是根基感。
许多基督徒正在寻找一些能让他们更深刻地感受到基督教历史信仰的稳定与联系的东西, 他们正在寻找有根的东西。 忏悔很容易成为我们研究的东西,
这是威斯敏斯特忏悔信仰的礼物之一. 其理论根源使几代信徒获得持久稳定,通过神学和文化变革的浪潮,使他们以历史信仰为基础。 并不只是教我们相信什么;
它将信仰植根于教会的生活中,将我们与几代忠实的基督徒联系起来,他们向我们坦白了同样的真理。 西敏的忏悔有助于我们发现我们不必靠自己找到基督教信仰的基础。
我们接受从我们之前的几代信徒那里学习的礼物,帮助我们更加清楚和自信地看见天经的丰富之处。 此卷是邀请人们重新发现这一遗产,并在上帝的忠诚中找到新的鼓励,上帝在几个世纪中一直维持着他的教堂.
愿它能帮助新一代人在改革后的传统财富中找到欢乐,并将它们充满信心地传给那些追随者。

articles.title: If the Church Did Its Job, Would the Parachurch Exist?
articles.summary: Do pregnancy centers, food pantries, or campus ministries exist because the church is failing to do her work?
articles.summary_zh: 我不止一次听到这样的话:“如果教会完成了它的任务,教区就不必存在。 ” 例如,我在咨询一位当地牧师,他希望看到教会为其社区的穷人服务。 对他来说重要的是,教会必须这样做,而不是一个非营利组织。 由于他明白上帝的王国比他的会众还大,他希望让多个教会参与这个项目.
articles.title_zh: 如果教会做了它的工作，教堂会存在吗？
articles.content: I’ve heard it said more than once: “If the church did its job, the parachurch wouldn’t have to exist.” For instance, I was consulting with a local pastor who wanted to see the church serve people in poverty in his community. It was important to him that the church do it, not a nonprofit. Since he understood that God’s kingdom is bigger than his congregation, he wanted to engage multiple churches in the project. I suggested he consider forming a council of pastors and collectively hiring a staff member to manage the operations of the combined program. He thought that could work well for his context. I’m not sure he was aware of the irony. I certainly was: We’d just reinvented a variant of the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that he so keenly wanted to avoid in the first place. While the allergy to faith-based nonprofits was especially strong in his case, many people accept the premise at a basic level. In my experience, this sentiment is just as likely to come from someone who works in nonchurch ministry as from a pastor. If we understand the church is the core institution created by Christ to advance the kingdom of heaven, has it failed so badly that we need an army of auxiliaries to prop it up? Clarifying Terms and Roles I answer that the parachurch doesn’t exist because the church has failed. It exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. Proving that starts with clarifying terms. The parachurch exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. “Church” has more than one use in Scripture. In some contexts, it describes the people of God universally (Matt. 16:15–18; Eph. 1:22–23; Col. 1:18). In others, it’s a local congregational institution with the parameters God has placed around its operation (1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:1–5; Philem. 1:2; James 5:14). “Parachurch” typically refers to faith-based nonprofits who serve people in need or provide evangelistic and discipleship resources. Certainly, as part of the universal church, all God’s people hold equal status in advancing God’s mission, whether they labor as nurses, students, pastors, or tentmakers (see Acts 18:1–3). Just as surely, all God’s people shouldn’t merely attend but be accountable to a local congregation that enables their spiritual formation. When not assembled, God’s people are charged with many tasks—everything from stewarding creation to seeking justice for the oppressed. We can fulfill these tasks as individuals, but it often makes sense to create or join institutions dedicated to fulfilling them. Which brings us to a crucial point: God ordained some institutions specifically, and some emerged organically from God’s commands. Ordained or Emergent Institutions The family, the local church, and the government are ordained institutions. The Bible gives each ordained institution some guidance but also leaves a lot open to interpretation. While these ordained institutions are necessary for all people, they aren’t sufficient to fulfill God’s myriad commands to their fullest extent. Thus, some institutions emerge from the commands, rather than from a revealed institutional structure: The command to work led to the formation of businesses. The command to pass knowledge to subsequent generations led to the formation of schools. The command to care for the sick caused Christians to form the first hospitals. The command to care for the poor, widows, orphans, and strangers led to the formation of charities . The command to make disciples of all nations led to mission boards, publishing houses, and Bible-translation ministries. This ordained-emergent distinction parallels Abraham Kuyper’s “ sphere sovereignty ” in its recognition of institutions not explicitly outlined in Scripture. Many of these commands can be fulfilled to some lesser degree by the ordained institutions, but there are limitations. A family may work without forming a business, but they’ll never raise a skyscraper. Most believers recognize that the bulk of emergent institutions are legitimate. No one says, “If the church did its job being hospitable, restaurants wouldn’t need to exist.” Similarly, I don’t hear a lot of people saying, “If the church cared for the sick, hospitals wouldn’t need to exist.” Businesses, schools, hospitals, and charities all work best when operated by believers in accordance with God’s precepts. But they don’t have to answer to a plurality of elders any more than they have to be structured like a family whose children must answer to their parents. Churches, Nonprofits, and Businesses Ordained institutions have distinct mandates that limit what other institutions should do. That’s why Paul instructs Timothy that the local church shouldn’t aid a widow who has a family capable of aiding her (1 Tim. 5:3–4). Without question, overeager nonprofits at times impinge on the core duties of a family or local church. But in general, emergent institutions are legitimate and complement the work of the government, congregation, and family. Ordained institutions have distinct mandates that limit what other institutions should do. The Bible acknowledges this by its support of businesses . While the command to work is ordained by God, Scripture nowhere defines a prescriptive business structure. Yet the employer-employee relationship is acknowledged as legitimate, and the institution as one that promotes human flourishing. Once for-profit entities aren’t viewed as a local congregation’s failure, the line between a kingdom-minded business and a kingdom-minded nonprofit becomes fuzzy. For instance, plenty of for- and nonprofit enterprises intentionally employ and disciple people who are difficult to employ. Surely the tax structure doesn’t determine the theological validity of the enterprise. Thus, claims like “God created the church; he didn’t create the pregnancy resource center”—while true in the most literal sense—don’t communicate much of value. It’s a bit like saying, “God made trees. He didn’t make your table.” My table is made almost entirely of trees. The table is a good thing for which I should be grateful to God. The parachurch exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. The more the church does its job, the more local congregations there will be, the more nonprofits there will be, and the more redemptive businesses there will be. The question isn’t whether the church should replace the parachurch but whether God’s people will faithfully build every institution needed to accomplish his will.

我不止一次听到这样的话:“如果教会完成了它的任务,教区就不必存在。 ” 例如,我在咨询一位当地牧师,他希望看到教会为其社区的穷人服务。 对他来说重要的是,教会必须这样做,而不是一个非营利组织。
由于他明白上帝的王国比他的会众还大,他希望让多个教会参与这个项目. 我建议他考虑成立一个牧师理事会,并集体雇用一名工作人员来管理合并方案的运作。 他认为这对他的背景来说是可行的。 我不确定他是否意识到讽刺。
我当然是:我们刚刚重塑了501(c)(3)非营利的变体, 虽然在他的案件中对基于信仰的非营利者的过敏特别强烈,但许多人在基本层面上接受了这一前提. 根据我的经验,这种情绪可能来自在非教会部工作的人和牧师。
如果我们理解教会是基督为推进天国而建立的核心机构,那么它是否失败得如此严重,以至于我们需要一支辅军来支撑它? 校对:Soup 它之所以存在,是因为上帝的命令自然会产生超越家庭、教会和国家的体制。
证明从澄清条款开始。 教区之所以存在,是因为上帝的命令自然会产生超越家庭、教会和国家的体制。 “教会”在《圣经》中有不止一种用途。 在某些情况下,它普遍描述了上帝的人民(Matt. 16:15–18;Eph. 1:22–23;Col. 1:18)。
在其他情况下,它是一个具有上帝设定参数的地方教会机构,围绕它的运作(1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:1–5; Philem. 1:2; James 5:14). “教区”通常指为有需要的人服务或提供福音和门徒资源的基于信仰的非营利组织。
当然,作为普世教会的一部分,所有上帝的人民在推进上帝的使命方面都享有平等地位,无论是作为护士、学生、牧师,还是帐篷制造者(见第18:1-3号法案)。 诚然,所有上帝的百姓不应该只参加,而应该对能够形成精神的当地教会负责。
在没有集合的时候,真主的百姓肩负着许多任务,从管理创造到为被压迫者寻求正义,都是全权负责的。 我们能够作为个人完成这些任务,但建立或加入专门履行这些任务的机构往往是合理的。 这使我们达到一个关键点:真主专门规定一些制度,有些制度是从真主的命令中有机地出现的。
组织或应急机构 家庭、地方教会和政府是法定机构。 《圣经》为每个指定机构提供了一些指导,但也为解释留下了许多余地。 虽然这些指定机构对所有人来说都是必要的,但它们不足以最充分地完成上帝的无数命令。
因此,有些机构来自指挥部,而不是一个公开的体制结构: 对工作的指挥导致了企业的形成. 将知识传递给后世的命令导致了学校的形成. 照顾病人的命令使得基督徒组成了第一批医院.
照顾穷人、寡妇、孤儿和陌生人的命令导致了慈善机构的成立。 使各国门徒的指挥导致了传教板,出版社,以及圣经翻译部. 这一规定性的区分与亚伯拉罕·库伊珀的 " 领域主权 " 相似,因为它承认《圣经》中没有明确概述的机构。
这些命令中有许多可以在较低程度上由指定机构执行,但也有局限性。 一家人可以工作而不创业, 大多数信徒承认,大多数新兴机构是合法的。
没有人会说,“如果教会做好了自己的工作,那么餐馆就不需要存在。 ” 类似地,我也没有听到很多人说,“如果教会照顾病人,医院就不需要存在。 ” 企业、学校、医院和慈善机构只要由信徒按照上帝的戒律运作,就都做得最好。
也不必像一个孩子必须向父母负责的家庭那样, 教会、非营利和经商机构有不同的授权,限制其他机构应做什么。
这就是为什么保罗指示蒂莫西, 当地教会不应该帮助一个有家庭能力帮助她的寡妇(1 Tim. 5: 3–4). 毫无疑问,过度掠夺的非营利组织有时会损害家庭或地方教会的核心职责。 但总的来说,新兴机构是合法的,是对政府、会众和家庭工作的补充。
法定机构有不同的授权,限制其他机构应做什么。 《圣经》通过支持企业来承认这一点。 虽然工作命令是由上帝下达的,但《圣经》却无一规定一种规范的商业结构。 然而,雇主与雇员的关系被公认为是合法的,而这种关系是促进人类繁荣的机构。
一旦盈利实体不被视为当地教会的失败,一个有王国意识的企业和一个有王国意识的非盈利之间的界线就会变得模糊不清。 例如,许多营利和非营利企业有意雇用难以雇用的人和门徒。 税收结构肯定不会决定企业的神学有效性。
因此,“上帝创建了教堂;他没有创建孕期资源中心”等说法,尽管从最直白的意义上讲,是真实的,但并没有传达多少价值。 这有点像说“上帝造树。 他没有给你做桌子。 我的桌子几乎全是树做的 桌子是件好事 我该感谢上帝
教区之所以存在,是因为上帝的命令自然会产生超越家庭、教会和国家的体制。 教会的工作越多,当地会众就会越多,非盈利性会越多,而红发的生意也会越多.

articles.summary: Joel Beeke joins Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan to explore what the Puritans can teach today’s pastors about prayer, preaching, personal holiness, shepherding souls, handling criticism, and persevering in ministry.
articles.summary_zh: 今天牧师能从清教徒那里学到什么? 马特·斯梅特赫斯特和利贡·邓肯欢迎乔尔·比克讨论清教徒牧师和神学家的持久智慧. 比克从几十年对清教徒的学习和教导中汲取经验,解释了为什么他们如此高度重视祷告,个人圣洁,并将经典应用于他们的会众的心和生活. 托玛·古德温 托玛斯·古德温 托玛斯·古德温 托玛斯·古德温 托玛斯·沃森 托玛斯·沃森 托玛斯·沃森 托玛斯·沃森 托玛斯·沃森 托玛斯·沃森 托玛斯·沃森 托玛斯·沃森

articles.content: What can pastors today learn from the Puritans? Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan welcome Joel Beeke to discuss the lasting wisdom of Puritan pastors and theologians. Drawing from decades of studying and teaching the Puritans, Beeke explains why they placed such a high priority on prayer, personal holiness, and applying Scripture to the hearts and lives of their congregations.
